<reason>Side B (PRO) wins by successfully defending the definitional core of populism as anti-pluralist and by reframing the debate from whether populists usually capture the state (where Side A has a point about selection bias) to whether the anti-pluralist logic itself constitutes democratic backsliding regardless of institutional constraints. Side B's rebuttal effectively answers the "denominator" challenge by arguing that populism is both symptom and pathogen—it signals existing decay and accelerates it through the erosion of mutual toleration, even when blocked by strong institutions. While Side A makes a compelling empirical case about the base rate of authoritarian outcomes, Side B demonstrates that the proposition holds even when populists fail to seize power, because the delegitimization of opponents as "enemies of the people" is itself a warning sign of institutional decay. Side B's structured rebuttals (A1/A2) directly neutralize Side A's pressure questions regarding definitional circularity and causation.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side B's Rebuttal 2 (A1/A2) decisively answering Side A's pressure questions by distinguishing populism's anti-pluralist logic from its win-loss record, arguing that moral exclusion of opponents constitutes backsliding even when institutions constrain the movement, and reframing populism as both symptom and pathogen rather than merely a reflection of institutional weakness.</best_rebuttal>
